02 · What I have done

NordicStays: a fabricated interface built for real behavioural research.

For my MSc thesis, I did not want participants' responses to be shaped by an existing booking brand. I therefore designed a fictional hotel-booking platform from scratch and used it as the experimental environment for a 2×2 between-subjects study.

I designed the brand identity, page layouts, icons, booking flow and urgency cues myself. The resulting platform, NordicStays, was deliberately realistic enough to support natural interaction while remaining fully controlled for experimental manipulation.

Interactive prototype → controlled study

NordicStays was not a mock-up for presentation. It was the experimental instrument.

The interface made it possible to manipulate specific design cues while holding the broader interaction context constant.

Explore the 4 experimental conditions →

Experimental design

Timer present/absent × scarcity message present/absent; randomised assignment; controlled exposure.

N = 69 valid participants after exclusions.

Behavioural measurement

Anxiety, perceived autonomy and satisfaction were measured using established scales and analysed quantitatively.

The study combined interaction design with empirical behavioural evaluation.

“The same design skills that can make a persuasive interface convincing can also be used to make an intervention testable.”
03 · Why this project

I became interested in autonomy because I learned how easy it is to influence it.

My transition from design practice to HCI research was not a move away from design. It was a move toward understanding its consequences.

During my design training and early professional experience, I learned how visual hierarchy, interaction flows and attention cues can guide people toward particular choices. The more I understood users, the more capable I became of designing interfaces that achieved a particular outcome.

That capability also made me increasingly interested in the boundary between helping a user act and shaping what the user chooses. My MSc research allowed me to investigate one part of that problem empirically through urgency cues, anxiety and perceived autonomy.

Human–AI Interaction brings the question into a new setting. When an AI system presents a recommendation, the interaction can become frictionless precisely at the point where a user might otherwise evaluate, question or verify information.

This is why the focus on safeguarding cognitive autonomy strongly resonates with my research trajectory. I am interested in understanding how interaction design can support human judgement rather than simply make AI-mediated decisions easier to accept.

DESIGN
Build the interaction.
Translate behavioural and user needs into an interface that people can actually interact with.
INTERVENE
Change the interaction deliberately.
Design a mechanism whose effect on users can be isolated and examined.
EVALUATE
Test what it changes.
Use controlled studies and mixed-method evidence to understand whether an intervention supports users' judgement.

I see the PhD as an opportunity to extend this empirical HCI approach from persuasive interface design to Human–AI Interaction, while developing stronger expertise in designing and evaluating interventions that support cognitive autonomy.
